title: Virtual memory
summary: Why processes get virtual addresses, from base and bounds to paging, how an address is translated, and how malloc manages the heap.

clips.title: Why virtual addresses?
clips.question: Why not let each process use physical addresses directly?

scenes.say: Virtual memory, question one. Why not let each process use physical memory addresses directly? What does the extra layer buy? Pause and answer out loud.

Three goals. Transparency: each process sees its own private address space, as if it had the machine to itself. Protection: a process can't even name another process's memory, let alone corrupt it. And efficiency: translation happens in hardware, on every access, so it has to be fast. The first hardware did it with base and bounds: add a base register to every address, and fault if it's past the bound.

items.label: Transparency
items.title: A private address space
items.body: Every process: the same layout, its own memory.

items.label: Protection
items.title: Isolation
items.body: Another process's memory can't even be named.

items.label: Efficiency
items.title: In hardware
items.body: Translated on every load and store.

items.label: Base and bounds
items.title: The first design
items.body: physical = virtual + base; fault past bound.

scenes.say: Base and bounds keeps the whole address space contiguous, including the empty gap between heap and stack. Segmentation gives each segment, code, heap and stack, its own base and bounds, so the gap costs nothing. But variable sized segments fragment physical memory, into holes too small to use. Paging cuts everything into fixed size pages. Any free frame fits any page, so external fragmentation disappears. That's what every modern system uses.

left.label: Segmentation
left.title: Variable-sized pieces
left.body: Base + bounds per segment. Physical memory fragments into unusable holes.

right.label: Paging
right.title: Fixed-size pages
right.body: Any free frame fits any page: no external fragmentation.

clips.title: Translating an address
clips.question: How does the hardware turn a virtual address into a physical one?

scenes.say: Question two. A load from a virtual address. How does the hardware turn it into a physical address? Pause and walk through it out loud.

Take a 32 bit address, with four kilobyte pages. The low twelve bits are the offset within the page. The top twenty bits are the virtual page number. The hardware uses the page number as an index into this process's page table, whose location sits in a register. The entry holds a physical frame number, plus control bits: present, writable, user, accessed, and dirty. The frame number replaces the page number, the offset is copied unchanged, and that's the physical address. If the entry isn't present, or the access breaks its permissions, the CPU raises a page fault instead.

nodes.label:
page table[0x00403]
frame 0x001FF · P W U A D

steps.note: Low 12 bits: offset within the page
Table location: a register (CR3 on x86)
Not present, or not allowed → page fault

scenes.say: This flat table has two problems. Space: two to the twenty entries, four bytes each, is four megabytes per process, mostly empty. And time: every load and store now needs an extra memory access, to read the entry first. Multi level tables fix the space, and the TLB fixes the time.

right.label: Time
right.title: An extra access
right.body: Read the entry before every load and store.

verdict.text: Multi-level tables fix space; the TLB fixes time.

clips.title: Inside malloc
clips.question: free() takes only a pointer. How does the allocator know how many bytes to free?

scenes.say: Question three. Free takes only a pointer, no size. So how does the allocator know how many bytes it's getting back? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: free() gets no size. How does it know?

scenes.say: The allocator hides a small header just before every block it hands out. Malloc takes a chunk from its free list, splitting a bigger one if needed, writes the size into the header, and returns the address just past it. Free steps back one header, and reads the size. A magic number catches pointers malloc never returned. The chunk goes back on the free list, and merges with free neighbours, so the heap doesn't crumble into small pieces.

props.title: A header before every block

highlights.note: Size lives in a hidden header
Take a chunk, splitting if needed
Return the address after the header

scenes.say: Which free chunk should it take? Best fit searches for the smallest that fits: little waste, but a slow search. First fit takes the first that fits: fast. Real allocators keep separate lists per size class, like the kernel's slab allocator for common objects. And the buddy allocator splits memory in powers of two, so a freed block merges with its buddy cheaply, at the cost of rounding sizes up. Big blocks skip all this: glibc maps them directly with m map, from 128 kilobytes by default.

items.label: Best fit
items.title: Smallest that fits
items.body: Little waste; searches the whole list.

items.label: First fit
items.title: First that fits
items.body: Fast; small fragments pile up at the front.

scenes.say: To recap. Virtual memory gives every process a private, protected address space. Paging uses fixed size pages, so any frame fits any page. A virtual address is a page number and an offset, and the page table maps the number to a frame. And malloc keeps each block's size in a header, just before the pointer.

Page number → frame; the offset is kept.
